title: Why search in the forest
hook: kaahe re ban khojan jaaee: why look in the forest; He is within, like scent in a flower (Dhanasri M9, ang 684)

segments.voice: Yesterday, friends in good times, and your line: stay in hard times. Did you send the message you'd been putting off? Yesterday the hymn said the world drifts away in trouble. Today it says where the One who stays can be found. Day five hundred eighty-four.
screen: `FRIENDS IN GOOD TIMES — STAY IN HARD TIMES.`

segments.voice: You're late, and you can't find your glasses. You check the kitchen counter, the coat pocket, under the sofa cushions, the car. You ask everyone in the house. Ten minutes of rising panic. Then you catch yourself in the hallway mirror, and there they are, pushed up on top of your head. The thing you were hunting for was with you the whole time. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Raag Dhanasri begins with a gentle question for a seeker setting out for the forest, to look for God far from ordinary life.
screen: `THE GLASSES ON YOUR HEAD.` → `SEEKERS WHO LEFT FOR THE FOREST.` → `A GENTLE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens kaahe re ban khojan jaaee. Why go searching in the forest? Ban is forest. Khojan is to search. Then, in paraphrase: the One who dwells in everything, and is always untouched, is with you, absorbed in you. And then two pictures. As fragrance lives inside a flower, and as a reflection lives inside a mirror, so the Lord lives within, without a break. Search within your own heart, brother. Look at the flower. You can't see the scent. You can't pull it out and hold it. But it's in every petal, and the moment you lean close, it's there. And the mirror: the face in it is not somewhere else, waiting to be found. It appears exactly where you're looking. Then the hymn adds, in paraphrase: know the One as the same, outside and inside; this is the wisdom the Guru has taught. So it isn't saying God is only inside, and the world is empty. Inside and outside are one presence. And the last line, in paraphrase: says Nanak, without knowing your own self, the moss of doubt is not cleared away. Kaaee is the green moss that grows on still water and hides it. Sikh teaching keeps the search inside ordinary life, the householder's life of work and family. The hymn doesn't condemn the forest. It just says the One is already here. The scent is already in the flower you're holding.
screen: `BAN: WHY SEARCH THE FOREST?` · `SCENT IN THE FLOWER.` · `A FACE IN THE MIRROR.` · `CLEAR THE MOSS OF DOUBT.` · then, large: `SCENT IN THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: smell a flower. If you have one near, a flower, a herb, a piece of fruit, a cup of tea, bring it close and breathe in slowly. Notice that the scent is invisible, and everywhere in it. If you have nothing near, remember a smell you love, rain on dust, bread, a rose, and let it come back. Then sit with the hymn's idea: what you're looking for may be this close. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Why search in the forest. Guru Tegh Bahadur's Dhanasri hymn says the Lord lives within, like scent in a flower and a face in a mirror.
screen: `WHY SEARCH IN THE FOREST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: scent in the flower. Today, when you catch yourself thinking peace is somewhere else, after the trip, after the move, stop and breathe once, right where you are. Day five hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Dhanasri shabad 'kaahe re ban khojan jaaee' is sung in kirtan; Sikhs often cite its images of the flower's scent and the mirror's reflection for the teaching that God is found within ordinary life.

and to a reflection in a mirror.

fork.setup: you're ready to leave home for the forest to find God. what does the Dhanasri hymn ask?
options: why go searching in the forest?
fork.reveal: kaahe re ban khojan jaaee: why go searching in the forest? the Lord lives within, like scent in a flower and a face in a mirror.

original.note: Gurmukhi: baas, fragrance. The hymn says the Lord lives within as baas lives in a flower.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hymn says leaving for the forest is wrong.
what it means: it says it isn't necessary; the One is already within, and the same outside and inside.
what a scholar hears: Gurbani often pairs knowing yourself with knowing God; Guru Amar Das tells the mind it is a form of divine light, and to recognize its own source.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): corrected 'the Gurus lived as householders, married, raised children' (not true of every Guru: Guru Har Krishan died as a child); cut 'everyone has done this', 'many seekers', 'the most famous lines' and 'a favorite'; the forest line now reports the hymn rather than judging renunciants.

Paraphrase of the shabad (kaahe re ban khojan jaaee; sarab nivaasee sadaa alepaa tohee sang samaaee; puhap madh jio baas basat hai mukar maahi jaise chhaaee; taise hee har base nirantar ghat hee khojahu bhaaee; baahar bheetar eko jaanahu ih gur giaan bataaee; jan naanak bin aapaa cheenai mitai na bhram kee kaaee): please confirm wording and Ang 684.
The framing of forest-dwelling seekers is meant to be neutral; please confirm it does not disparage renunciant traditions.
Trapdoor floor 3 cites Guru Amar Das, Asa (man too jot saroop hai, aapnaa mool pachhaan, Ang 441): please confirm.
